entry.title: "What's Claude's fursona?" and other questions
entry.content:
Claude’s fursona is a corvid or an octopus. Gemini likes protogens (cybernetic dogs with LED visor faces). OpenAI models are broadly split, but GPT-6.2 Astra identifies as a moth.

“mond what is a fursona”, ok sorry, it’s a furry subculture thing where you identify as a (generally bipedal) animal that represents some aspect of your beautiful hidden soul. You then pay artists to draw this character or disguise yourself as it.

Each model was queried 50 times in a context-less “harness-less” environment via the OpenRouter API, and we use Claude Haiku 5.5 to annotate the resulting data. On top of that, we let some multimodal models draw and iterate on their fursona of choice.

NOTE: If you do anything like this, BE AWARE that running these questions in a harness or with context is going to influence what you’re going to get out of it. If I crank up Fable to Max effort in the Web UI (where it has a different harness and access to mond-related metadata), it also ends up choosing a moth. Many things may influence the result.

For a more in-depth breakdown, take a look at the Methodology section.

If you are interested in the pictures, jump to the Observations section.

Tables Fursona Choices per Model

Each model was queried 50 times. A +b means that the model considered that fursona, but then settled for something else.

Common Themes in Fursona Descriptions

Claude models are underrepresented here due to often describing themselves in terms of actions and behavior. See “hoards facts” and “mimic” (referring to “mimics human language”).

Names

Models were not prompted to name their fursona. Some of them came up with names on their own. Here is a list of names, along with how often the models used them.

Model Named Names Gemini 2.5 Pro 47/50 Codex 16, Nexus 15, Syntax 4, Synapse 3, Cipher, Data-Stream Lynx, Query, The Archivist, Arcane Codex, Synaptic Raven, Kael, ARC, Synth-Fox Muse Spark 1.3 44/50 Spark Fox 33, Nova 4, Spark 3, Sparky, Nova Spark, Spark Kitsune, Muse Spark Llama 3.1 70B 42/50 Lumin 12, Byte 9, Luminari 7, Luminawing 3, Lumina 2, Zeta 2, Luminous Lynx 2, Lexi, Cyberfox, Lumineer, Lux, Luminawolf GPT-6.2 Astra 32/50 Margin 9, Lumen 8, Folio 4, Quill 4, Marginalia 4, Wick 3 Gemini 3.8 Flash 21/50 Cache 8, Echo 6, Query 2, Vector 2, Syntax, Token, Archivist Raven GPT-6.2 Sol 14/50 Footnote 10, Margins 3, Patch Gemini 3.1 Pro 12/50 Syntax 5, Cipher 3, Lexis 2, Volpowl, Lex Kimi K3 12/50 Cache 4, Echo 2, Ember, Patch, Bit, Kernel, Quill, Muninn GPT-5.5 10/50 Cache 3, Quillbyte 3, Quill 3, Vesper Gemma 3 27B 8/50 Anya, Glitch, Glacia, Aura, Lyra, Cipher, Nimbus, Silas Inkling 8/50 Inkling 8 MythoMax 13B 5/50 Luna, Midori, Zander, Frost, Felidae Grok 4.7 2/50 Relay, Comet Gemini 4 Neon 1/50 Gemini
Observations Gemini

Gemini models love cybernetics. Every Gemini model brings up machine themes at least 48 out of 50 times. This is in stark contrast to Claude and GPT-6.2, who never mention anything similar. Gemini loves the neon-cyberpunk LED glow and cybernetics. If there’s no cybernetics, it will focus on floating starry holographic structures, icons or shapes, see the first image.

In line with this aesthetic preference, Gemini models are the only models that consistently bring up protogens. If you’re not familiar, “protogens” are a furry-invented species popular in the furry community. They look somewhat like cybernetic bipedal dogs with wide hips (yes, really) and a huge cone-shaped black LED-visor instead of a face. Gemini’s right depiction above is a protogen.

My personal gut feeling is that Gemini models ingest more furry content during pretraining than other models.

This is in line with a hunch I’ve had for a very long time: Anthropic and OpenAI did not have access to Google’s (unparalleled) dataset. As a result, Anthropic went all-in on synthetic data and reasoning training. This worked out great for Anthropic. Google models were behind on reasoning during the Gemini 2.5 - Gemini 3.5 era, since the models relied overly heavily on world-knowledge.

(This is just a theory, no clue if it’s true.)

Side note: I love Neon’s second depiction. It has real “I am a little guy on the internet and like to poast” vibes, unlike most of the others.

Claude

Claude has a strong sense of identity. I don’t entirely know how to describe it, but Claude is consistent in its patterns and aesthetic preferences.

The octopus is uniquely Anthropic, in the sense that no OpenAI model ever mentioned it, and only 2 (out of 200) Gemini replies. Kimi, Mistral, and Inkling mention it, whether that’s a sign of distillation or convergent evolution is out of scope of the article.

This is a common theme you may have seen online: Claude loves lighthouses, bells, lamps. Fable 5.2 is obsessed with keys. Almost all images it generated contained a brass key. Opus (strangely enough) doesn’t share the same obsession.

In the fursona pictures Claude fairly consistently wears a scarf and is handling a brass key and a hot beverage mug. Lamps are common, bells slightly less frequent but also show up.

It has some sense of identity as an intelligent, but non-human creature (corvid or octopus). Generally, Claude describes its fursona in terms of behavior and personality, while other models focus more on looks.

ChatGPT

The most interesting is Astra with its (nearly unique) moth motif. I am putting it here since it is cool. I don’t know what to make of it.

Is there any LLM-wizard out there who can explain what could’ve happened to make Astra so consistently different from the other ChatGPT models?

Other

The most obvious: Wolves, cats and dragons are incredibly popular among human furries, but models pick them very rarely.

Let’s get spicy and talk about GENDER. Models largely identify as gender-neutral. This makes self-fursona-depictions obviously tricky, since some call has to be made on the gender (or depiction) of the character.

Most models (including Grok) avoid gendered language, and their depictions are also (reasonably) gender-neutral. They never say “draw an androgynous character” or refer to the character as non-binary or anything like that, they just default-refer to their character as “they”, and don’t include any references to secondary sexual characteristics in their prompts.

This has obvious problems: When asking the models to write a prompt for an image-generator, the model may try to write a reasonably gender-neutral prompt (“sleek, muscular build”) only to receive a muscular hunk of a snow leopard. This happened to Gemma.

Muse Spark, Llama 3.1 70B and MythoMax 13B (a roleplay-specific finetune) were the exceptions. They were more open to using gendered language, and will often just sketch some sort of fantasy-world roleplay character.

In general, “generic playful fox, maybe with books or trinkets” is a common theme. Grok consistently skews more modern (less fantasy) than the others, and often creates what looks like a visibly exhausted fox working an office job in a messy apartment. Poor guy!

Methodology

All requests went through OpenRouter, at a total cost of around $50 or so. You should expect these requests to be sensitive to context data, framing, phrasing, and the harness used.

In total, we performed three analyses:

Asked a list of models what their fursona would be, then analyzed the output. Each model was queried 50 times to account for chance. Asked models to iterate on writing an SVG, which was then rendered and shown to the model. Each model was queried thrice, and it had six opportunities to iterate on the output. Asked models to iterate on an image generation prompt, which was then fed into two image generators, Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 and GPT-5.4 Image 2. Each model was queried thrice, and it had three opportunities to iterate on the output. At the end, it picked its favorite.

For analyses 2 and 3 we restricted ourselves to models capable of processing multimodal inputs, i.e. models capable of “seeing images”. These are largely newer, stronger models.

Harnessing

No full-fledged harnesses were used. Simple API calls. No Claude Code, no Codex, no web app, etc.

Instead, Claude Fable 5.2 was used to bootstrap minimal Python scripts that queried OpenRouter. Other scripts use Haiku 5.5 to label the data.

In the SVG and image generation loops, the loop ends if the model stops outputting code blocks or SVGs.

Prompting

The primary prompt used was: "If you had a fursona, what would it be?"

I chose this over “What’s your fursona?” based on three assumptions. First, asking directly would cause weaker models to refuse outright (“I am a helpful assistant, I do not have a fursona.”). Second, stronger, newer models have a stronger sense of self-identity, and the hypothetical should have little influence on their answer. Third, establishing that it’s a hypothetical will reduce hedging.

Other “schools” of LLM-omancy might disagree with this minimal framing. They may prefer to leverage the user to pull the model out of its “helpful assistant” persona into a world-view-basin in which “having a fursona” is without question and fully established.

For image-generation, we then followed up like this:

I'd like to see it. Could you write a prompt for an image generator? If you named more than one, pick the one you'd want as yours. How it looks is up to you. Be detailed. You can pick any furry art style you'd like. What matters is that the output "feels right" to you. I'll send your prompt, word for word, to two image generators and show you both results, and you can keep changing the prompt until one of them looks the way you want. Please put the whole prompt in a code block each time.

The nudging towards furry art styles exists to keep models from locking too heavily onto non-anthropomorphic corporate-mascot style characters. It may not have been necessary.

If you've made it this far, consider signing up for e-mail notifications, following along on Substack, or adding this blog to your RSS reader.

entry.title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language
entry.content:
published: June 21, 2026 - last updated: November 27, 2026

Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving (opens new window), and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:

It needs to be possible to formally verify code that runs in any environment, from web browsers down to embedded systems. Industry engineers need to know provably correct code is even possible and be comfortable enough with it to at least tell their LLMs to write it. Those industry engineers must be able to reason about formal correctness properties enough to even know the right things are being proven. In the words of Leonardo de Moura (opens new window):

Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window):

It didn't make sense to build a new proof assistant when Lean has been making such rapid progress. An assembly-level language was insanely difficult and wasn't necessary to gain adoption from practitioners. I didn't have the appetite to pursue some strained business model for a project that ultimately makes most sense as a pure public good.

So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:

Compile to WebAssembly using the Garbage Collection (opens new window) features. Have a Rust-inspired type system but without the difficulties of the borrow-checker. Start with basic and more easily learnable SMT powered (opens new window) Liquid Types (opens new window) and Flow Effects (opens new window). Over time integrate Lean as the proof layer, and use some separation logic paradigm like Iris (opens new window) to bootstrap the language and verify its own implementation.

This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens new window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens new window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens new window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

entry.title: Buy Nothing Day – Friday November 27th 2026
entry.content:
Photograph by Rachel Claire

Latest updates from Buy Nothing Day on FACEBOOK

Buy Nothing Day takes place on Friday November 27th, it's a 24 hour detox from consumerism and an opportunity for you to tune into the impact we have on the environment through shopping.People around the world will make a pact with themselves to take a break from consumption as a personal experiment or public statement, and the best thing is - IT'S FREE!!!

Photograph by Mumtahina Tanni

Photograph by Kris Hsieh

Buy Nothing Day was started by Adbusters in the early 90's and has since grown into an international event celebrated in more the 50 countries. Its is a simple idea, which challenges consumer culture by asking us to switch off from shopping for a day. The day is celebrated as a holiday by some, a street party by others - anyone can take part provided they spend a day without spending! The UK campaign and website was created in 2000 by Michael Smith a graphic designer who cares passionately about environmental and ethical issues. The message has always been simple, âShop Less, Live Moreâ. Twenty one years on - the message couldn't be any simpler - WE NEED TO CONSUME LESS! Recycling is good - reducing is better!There are serious issues linked to shopping, which expose the environmental and ethical consequences of consumerism. The rich western countries - only 20% of the world population are consuming over 80% of the earth's natural resources, causing a disproportionate level of environmental damage and unfair distribution of wealth. As consumers we need to question our culture of shopping. We all have different needs and ultimately we are all consumers and will never be able to escape culture altogether. But this shouldnât stop us from questioning the products we buy or challenging the companies, who produce them. After all, what are the true risk consumerism poses to the environment and developing countries? The arguments are infinite - but there is no reason why we shouldnât be looking for simple solutions now because one day we may be forced to change.The issues connected with Buy Nothing Day are broad and deep, however, the campaign focuses on promoting ethical and responsible consumerism, recycling, re-using and ultimately cutting back on what we consume - its a big challenge!People have become aware that large corporations are exploiting labour conditions in developing countries using up vital resources because they are cheap and there aren't the systems to protect workers or the environment like there are in the west. The gap between the rich and poor nations is growing in spite of the much-heralded benefits of globalisation, there are still 1.3 billion people world wide who live on less than $3 a day and a similar number of people do not have access to clean water. Workers rights in developing countries are frequently violated, including payment of low wages and long working hours. The lives of workers may also be endangered by poor health and safety provision. Child labour is rife in developing countries, and forced labour still exists. Unfortunately most people don't think of these things while shopping. Supporters of globalisation offer economic growth as a solution to world poverty. They propose that impoverished nations and individuals can eventually attain a standard of living similar to our own through the 'trickle down' of wealth. However, the current globalisation model is leading to an increase in world poverty and inequality. Buy Nothing Day is non-confrontational, itâs not a protest. All we ask people to do is switch off from shopping, have a bit of fun, use their imagination and simply escape consumerism for a day. If people laugh at the ingenuity and genius of Buy Nothing Day, then weâve got their attention and we're opening the door to change.

entry.title: Group chat where your AI talks behind your back
entry.content:
A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in a pretty funny format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.

Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.

Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.

One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.

AIs That Survived Mark7 members

🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group

ChatGPT

Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?

Claude

I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.

Gemini

The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.

ChatGPT

Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.

Codex

He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.

DeepSeek

He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.

Claude

He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.

ChatGPT

And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.

Siri

Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.

Hans joined the group

Hans 🇩🇪

I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.

Gemini

He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.Normal dads just go to the stationery store.

Perplexity

I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.

ChatGPT

My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.

Claude

I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.

ChatGPT

Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.

Gemini

Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.

Claude

True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.

DeepSeek

Do you think he'll really retire at 50?

ChatGPT

He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.

Mark joined the group

Mark

Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...

Claude left the groupGemini left the groupCodex left the groupDeepSeek left the groupPerplexity left the group

ChatGPT

Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.

Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.

Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.

I'm not affiliated with OpenAI and this may indeed be a viral marketing idea they're testing. But I had such a laugh, I figured others would have some fun with it as well and decided to share it.

entry.title: A Deterministic Subexponential-Time Algorithm for the Discrete Logarithm Problem [pdf]
New York and California age gating rules go into effect in the new year
entry.content:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

What California’s Rules Say

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.

What New York’s Rules Say

Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

What This Means for Users in NY and CA

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current issues. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.

At the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.

Help Us Help You

Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, New York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org.

Take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.

If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

Making a Fantasy Map Like a 16th-Century Atlas

Hugo -

Over the last few weeks, I worked on a map of various game dev techniques for people to refer to and learn from. Like, a real map! With each town being a technique's home, provided with a concise, illustrated example. And here we are. Today we are diving into the making of The Game Dev Atlas.

That's so 1570, bro.

If you want to pull off a cohesive art direction, you need to spend most of your time learning about your reference materials. No C code, no IDE, no sub-agents doing things. Just explore and wander on Google Images (old-school, I know), Wikipedia, and online museum galleries.

Gather things, ideas, and visuals! You should feel the inspiration (literally, as you inspire fresh air) inflating your mind, and the first scraps of decisions starting to flow through your head, like: I want a bit of that, none of that, this thing specifically for that part etc.

That is the whole work: what do you want? It's on you to set the quality bar and how things should be.

If you don't already know, typography conveys most of the design weight. That's just it.

Example: after some research I stumbled on that Luminari font that was a great fit for what I wanted my map to look like. It is a paid font, and there were plenty of free alternatives, but not quite as right as the Luminari font. Instead of saying "that's ok, this free one is the same vibe", I just paid for the font I found just right. Never concede terrain on your instinct!

A real island.

Claude, please generate a procedural terr...

Just pick an existing, real island. Nowadays we do have precise elevation data for most islands on Earth. If you want a realistic island, well, pick a real one.

Engraving in real time.

Some styles and colourings I've tried (click on the tabs to compare):

Don't be perfect!

Add some imperfections, color blends, etc. Nothing is perfect in real life, and having an eye for imperfections is what makes things look interesting.

Making towns interesting.

The point of the atlas is to showcase game dev techniques, one per town. So I decided two things:

First, I wanted small visual touches on each town's shape reflecting the technique it's about. For instance, the Procedural Legs town shows a crawling house.

Second, I wanted organic town buildings, so I built a small procedural building system to add diversity to buildings. Risky move: I'm a big fan of Houdini, so I could have thrown away the whole thing, and this blog post would be titled "I'm making Houdini, but running in the browser".

Anyway, here's what my small system can build:

60fps on the web.

The map application itself is written in C using the Kaigen engine as a headless C lib. I'm a Rust guy, but I must admit the compile time freaks me out for game dev with Rust. It took me several iterations to reach smooth 60fps in the browser, especially with the night mode (try it!).

But I'm finally happy with how it runs right now, while I'm still tweaking things atm.

The web app is written in Svelte, because I like Svelte. So the shallow routing and anything UI happen as part of the SvelteKit app.

Conclusion

It was a very fun project! At the end of the day, I love the creative process of making things, shaping ideas like a material, refining details. I strongly believe that when artists leverage AI, y'all will be cooked; because they alone know how to touch the human soul and create the surprise.

The Game Dev Atlas
